passages.title: Marks 2006 Risk Memo
passages.section: Measuring risk before and after the fact
passages.text:
- Looking forward, risk is an opinion. There is no standard way to put a number on it, and rare "improbable disasters" make investments look safer than they are (he quotes Nassim Taleb on Russian roulette with a huge revolver).
- Looking back, risk still can't be measured. Something happening does not mean it was likely; something not happening does not mean it was unlikely.
- Taleb's "alternative histories": was a winner skilful or lucky? A weather forecaster's 70% chance of rain can't be judged from one day. Judging risk-adjusted performance takes skilled, subjective judgment, not precise volatility ratios.

passages.title: Marks 2006 Risk Memo
passages.text:
- Keynes: a speculator knowingly runs risks; an investor runs risks without knowing it. Unknowingly bearing risk in popular, "can't-lose" assets is the big mistake. Knowingly accepting recognised risk at the right price is behind many of the best investments.
- Life-insurance analogy (his answer to a reporter about junk bonds): insurers know everyone will die, yet they are conservative businesses. The risk is known, can be analysed, can be diversified and is well paid for. Oaktree tries to do the same with high-yield bonds.
- Risky assets can be good investments if they are cheap enough; the skill is knowing when.
- Risk control is not risk avoidance. Avoiding all risk also means avoiding returns above the risk-free rate. The aim is "risk intelligence": understanding, managing and being paid for the risks you take.

passages.title: Buffett 1993 Letter
passages.text:
- Buffett and Munger decided long ago that it is too hard to make hundreds of smart decisions in a lifetime. Their strategy requires being smart only a few times; he says they will now settle for one good idea a year.
- Many experts would call this concentrated strategy riskier. Buffett disagrees. Concentration can *reduce* risk if it makes the investor think harder about a business and demand more comfort with its economics before buying.
- He defines risk using the dictionary: the possibility of loss or injury.

passages.title: Marks 2006 Risk Memo
passages.section: Why risk matters, and the misread risk-return line
passages.text:
- Capital-market theory: because people dislike risk, riskier investments must offer higher returns to attract money. Returns should be judged relative to the risk taken (risk-adjusted returns).
- The usual chart shows a line rising from low risk/low return to high risk/high return. Marks objects to the popular reading, "take more risk to make more money." If riskier investments reliably produced higher returns, they would not be riskier.
- The correct version: riskier investments must offer higher *expected* or *promised* returns, but nothing guarantees those returns will arrive.
- His redrawn chart shows, at each risk level, a range of possible outcomes that widens as risk rises. Higher risk brings a higher expected return, a chance of lower returns, and sometimes a chance of loss.

reply:
Here is a 3-bullet study plan on risk, based on your notes:

*   **Understand the Nature of Risk:** Focus on the idea that risk is primarily an opinion, not a fixed number. Recognize that events don't automatically imply probability, and judging risk requires skilled, subjective judgment rather than precise volatility ratios [S1].
*   **Distinguish Between Speculation and Investing:** Contrast knowingly running risks (speculation) with unknowingly bearing risk (investing). Emphasize that the mistake is unknowingly accepting risk in assets marketed as "can't-lose," and that intelligent risk management involves understanding, managing, and being paid for the risks you take, rather than just avoidance [S2].
*   **Evaluate Risk-Adjusted Returns:** Shift your focus from simply taking more risk for higher returns to analyzing risk-adjusted returns. Remember that riskier investments must offer higher *expected* or *promised* returns, but those returns are not guaranteed, and the relationship between risk and return is not a simple linear line [S4].

passages.title: Marks 2003 Most Important Thing
passages.text:
- Mainstream large-cap stock markets are fairly efficient, so active fees rarely earn their keep there. Inefficient markets — uneven information, few or non-objective investors, specialised expertise needed — allow real mispricings. In those markets low risk and high return can go together. Marks chose to work only in inefficient markets.
- Be wary of leverage. It raises potential return but also raises risk and removes the margin of safety. It is acceptable to exploit unusually generous opportunities, but dangerous for squeezing big returns out of thin margins.
- Much of short-term performance is out of anyone's control: competitors, the environment and luck. Something probable may not happen, and something that happened may have been improbable. Judging managers therefore can't be purely quantitative.

- The usual chart shows a line rising from low risk/low return to high risk/high return. Marks objects to the popular reading, "take more risk to make more money." If riskier investments reliably produced higher returns, they would not be riskier.

passages.title: Buffett 1987 Letter
passages.section: Mr. Market as a business partner
passages.text:
- He retells Ben Graham's allegory. Imagine market quotes coming from an emotional partner, Mr. Market, who offers every day to buy your share of a business or sell you his.
- Mr. Market's mood swings between euphoria (very high prices) and depression (very low prices), even when the underlying business is stable.
- You are free to ignore him; he will return tomorrow with a new price. The more erratic his moods, the better for the investor.
- The key warning: Mr. Market is there to serve you, not to guide you. His prices are useful; his opinions are not. If you cannot value your business better than he can, you should not be playing.
- Buffett says success comes from combining good business judgment with the ability to keep your thinking insulated from market emotion, not from formulas, computer models or price signals.
- He judges holdings by their operating results, not by daily or yearly quotes. He repeats Graham's idea that in the short run the market is a voting machine and in the long run a weighing machine. Slow recognition by the market can even help, because it allows buying more at bargain prices.

passages.title: Marks 2003 Most Important Thing
passages.text:
- Above all, the relationship between price and value matters. No asset is so good it can't be a bad investment at too high a price, and few are so bad they can't be good investments if cheap enough.
- No asset class has a birthright to high returns. You'd ask the price before buying someone's car, so buying an investment without judging its price is just as silly. Examples: tech stocks in the late 1990s (bought at any price) and junk bonds in the 1970s-80s (avoided at any price).
- The biggest losses he has seen came from buying "perfect" companies at prices that assumed perfection. A good company is not the same as a good investment.
- He wants the best *buys*, not the best companies.

reply:
Here is a shorter summary of what Howard Marks said about investing in high valuation markets:

*   **Focus on Inefficient Markets:** Marks prefers working in inefficient markets where information is uneven or expertise is specialized, as these environments allow for real mispricings and the potential for low risk and high return [S1].
*   **Be Wary of Leverage:** Leverage increases potential returns but also raises risk and removes the margin of safety [S1].
*   **Risk-Adjusted Returns Matter:** The idea that you can "take more risk to make more money" is flawed. Instead, riskier investments must offer higher *expected* or *promised* returns, and you must judge returns relative to the risk taken [S2].
*   **Price vs. Value is Paramount:** The relationship between price and value is key. No asset is so good it can't be a bad investment at too high a price, and you must judge the price before buying [S4].
